examples.en: Speaking of moving — if you know a good place, let me know.
examples.note: Riding a topic into a small request

entries.nuance: Spoken segue that piggybacks on a topic someone just raised, so your follow-up feels natural rather than out of the blue. The fuller 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 ('since it came up, here's what I'll say') often precedes a candid remark or request. Casual-polite; shorten to 말 나온 김에 with friends.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Use it only when the topic genuinely just came up; to switch to an unrelated topic, use 그건 그렇고.
It's a lead-in — follow it with the actual point you want to add.

entries.explanation: 다행이네요 (dahaengineyo) means "Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다 잘 끝났다니 다행이네요. examples.en: A: I thought I lost my wallet, but it was in my bag. B: Oh good!

entries.nuance: Warm, genuine reaction expressing relief — 다행 means 'good fortune,' so it's 'how fortunate.' Said to others it reads as caring ('I'm relieved for you'); about your own situation it's 'phew.' Casual-polite as 다행이네요/다행이에요; drop to 다행이다 with friends. The -네요 adds a touch of heartfelt spontaneity.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling is 다행 (多幸); don't write 다행히 here — 다행히 is the adverb 'fortunately.'
It's about relief, not congratulations; for an achievement use 축하해요 instead.

entries.english: Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)
entries.shortExplanation: 큰일 났다 is a practical expression meaning "Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)".
entries.explanation: "Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)" — that is 큰일 났다 (keunil natda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 큰일 났다, 지갑을 집에 두고 왔어. ("Oh no, I left my wallet at home."). entries.nuance: High-alarm reaction literally meaning 'a big thing has happened' — said when you realize something's gone wrong or is about to. Tone ranges from genuine panic to a half-joking 'uh-oh.' 큰일 났다/났어 with friends, 큰일 났어요 in polite speech; 큰일 나다 in future/conditional warns of looming trouble. Often paired with 어떡해 ('what do I do').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Keep the spacing 큰일 났다 (큰일 is one noun).
Don't use it for minor inconveniences; it implies a real problem (even if exaggerated for effect).

entries.english: Oh no, what to do / Oh dear / How awful (sympathetic worry, often on someone's behalf)
entries.shortExplanation: 어쩌나 is a practical expression meaning "Oh no, what to do / Oh dear / How awful (sympathetic worry, often on someone's behalf)".
entries.explanation: 어쩌나 (eojjeona) = "Oh no, what to do / Oh dear / How awful (sympathetic worry, often on someone's behalf)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 아이고, 어쩌나. ("Oh dear, what to do."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 어쩌나 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Oh no, what now — the tickets are all sold out.
usagePhrases.note: 이를 어쩌나 = 'what to do about this'

usagePhrases.en: I was worried, but it sorted itself out.
You have to go alone? Oh dear.

examples.ko: A: 감기가 안 낫네요. B: 어쩌나, 병원은 가 보셨어요?
examples.romanization: A: gamgiga an nanneyo. B: eojjeona, byeongwoneun ga bosyeosseoyo?
examples.en: A: My cold won't go away. B: Oh no — have you seen a doctor?

examples.ko: 짐이 이렇게 많은데 비까지 오니 어쩌나.
examples.romanization: jimi ireoke maneunde bikkaji oni eojjeona.
examples.en: So much luggage and now it's raining too — what to do.
I was on edge, worried about being late to the interview.

entries.nuance: Soft exclamation of worry or sympathy — 'oh dear, what's to be done.' It's gentler and more tender than 큰일 났다, often directed at someone else's predicament, and warm rather than panicked. It can stand alone as a reaction or sit inside a sentence ('worried that…'). Slightly soft/caring in tone; 어쩌지 is a near-synonym for your own dilemma.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It expresses concern, not blame — don't aim it at someone as criticism.
Standalone 어쩌나 is a feeling, not a real question; if you actually want advice, ask 어떻게 하죠?

entries.english: That can happen / It's possible, I guess / Fair enough (accepting something as understandable)
entries.shortExplanation: 그럴 수도 있죠 is a practical expression meaning "That can happen / It's possible, I guess / Fair enough (accepting something as understandable)".
entries.explanation: 그럴 수도 있죠 (geureol sudo itjyo) means "That can happen / It's possible, I guess / Fair enough (accepting something as understandable)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 뭐, 그럴 수도 있죠. ("Well, that can happen, I suppose."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 그럴 수도 있죠 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Well, that can happen, I suppose.
That can happen — everyone makes mistakes.
I suppose that could be the case.

examples.ko: A: 제가 깜빡하고 답장을 안 했어요. B: 괜찮아요, 그럴 수도 있죠.
examples.romanization: A: jega kkamppakago dapjangeul an haesseoyo. B: gwaenchanayo, geureol sudo itjyo.
examples.en: A: I forgot to reply. B: It's okay, that happens.

examples.ko: A: 그 사람이 오해했나 봐요. B: 그럴 수도 있죠, 설명이 부족했으니까요.
examples.romanization: A: geu sarami ohaehaenna bwayo. B: geureol sudo itjyo, seolmyeongi bujokaesseunikkayo.
examples.en: A: I think they misunderstood. B: That's possible — the explanation was lacking.

examples.ko: 처음이라 긴장했어요. 그럴 수도 있죠, 뭐.
examples.romanization: cheoeumira ginjanghaesseoyo. geureol sudo itjyo, mwo.
examples.en: I was nervous since it was my first time. That's only natural, I guess.
examples.note: Trailing 뭐 adds an easygoing shrug

entries.nuance: Easygoing, accepting phrase meaning 'that's within the realm of normal — no big deal.' Use it to forgive a minor mistake, validate someone's feeling, or concede that a possibility is reasonable. The -죠 ending invites soft mutual agreement. Casual-polite; 그럴 수도 있지 with friends. Generous in tone, the opposite of 말도 안 돼요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't use it to dismiss something serious — it signals 'understandable,' so it can sound flippant about a real problem.
그럴 수도 있죠 (accepting it happened) differs from 그럴 리가 없죠 ('no way that's true').

entries.english: I think that'd be best / You'd better do that / That sounds like the way to go (gently recommending)
entries.shortExplanation: 그러는 게 좋겠어요 is a practical expression meaning "I think that'd be best / You'd better do that / That sounds like the way to go (gently recommending)".
entries.explanation: "I think that'd be best / You'd better do that / That sounds like the way to go (gently recommending)" — that is 그러는 게 좋겠어요 (geureoneun ge jokesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요. ("Yes, I think that'd be best."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 그러는 게 좋겠어요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Yes, I think that'd be best.
usagePhrases.note: Agreeing that a suggested course is wise

usagePhrases.en: If you're tired, you'd better rest a bit.
It'd be best to book in advance.
I don't think you should do that.

examples.ko: A: 비도 오는데 그냥 집에 있을까요? B: 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: bido oneunde geunyang jibe isseulkkayo? B: ne, geureoneun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: A: It's raining — should we just stay home? B: Yes, I think that'd be best.

examples.ko: A: 의사한테 한번 물어볼까요? B: 그러는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: uisahante hanbeon mureobolkkayo? B: geureoneun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Should I ask the doctor? B: That'd be the way to go.

examples.ko: 오늘은 일찍 자는 게 좋겠어요, 내일 일찍 일어나야 하니까요.
examples.romanization: oneureun iljjik janeun ge jokesseoyo, naeil iljjik ireonaya hanikkayo.
examples.en: You'd better sleep early today, since you have to get up early tomorrow.

entries.nuance: Polite, gentle recommendation — V-는 게 좋겠다 literally 'it'd be good if (you/we) did ~,' i.e., 'had better.' The -겠- makes it a soft suggestion rather than an order, so it advises without bossing. 그러는 게 좋겠어요 specifically endorses a course already on the table ('yes, let's do that'). Casual as 그러는 게 좋겠어.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's advice, not a command — for a firm instruction use V-(으)세요.
Spacing: 그러는 게 (게 = 것이 contracted), written as a separate word.

entries.english: Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')
entries.shortExplanation: 마음대로 하세요 is a practical expression meaning "Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')".
entries.explanation: 마음대로 하세요 (maeumdaero haseyo) = "Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 편하실 대로 마음대로 하세요. ("Please do whatever's comfortable for you."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 마음대로 하세요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Please do whatever's comfortable for you.
usagePhrases.note: Warm version — genuinely leaving it to them
마음대로 해 = casual; tone decides if it's kind or curt

usagePhrases.en: Help yourself, eat as much as you like.
Then do whatever you want, see if I care.

examples.ko: A: 여기 앉아도 돼요? B: 그럼요, 마음대로 하세요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi anjado dwaeyo? B: geureomyo, maeumdaero haseyo.
examples.en: A: Can I sit here? B: Of course, make yourself at home.
Order whatever you like — it's on me.
examples.note: Generously leaving the choice to them

examples.ko: A: 그냥 내 방식대로 할게요. B: …마음대로 하세요.
examples.romanization: A: geunyang nae bangsikdaero halgeyo. B: …maeumdaero haseyo.
examples.en: A: I'll just do it my way. B: …Suit yourself.

entries.nuance: Means 'do it however you wish' (마음 = mind/heart, -대로 = 'in accordance with'). Tone is everything: said warmly it's generous ('go right ahead, no need to ask'); said flatly or with a sigh it turns into a frosty 'fine, do what you want, I give up.' Casual-polite as 마음대로 하세요; 마음대로 해 with friends. The friendly 마음껏 ('to your heart's content') never carries the cold edge.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Be careful with tone — to a senior or in tension it can sound dismissive or rude.
Spelling: 마음대로 (one word, no space before 대로); don't write 맘대로 in formal contexts (it's a casual contraction).

entries.english: for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')
entries.shortExplanation: 발등에 불 떨어지다 is a practical expression meaning "for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')".
entries.explanation: 발등에 불 떨어지다 (baldeunge bul tteoreojida) means "for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 발등에 불 떨어져서 밤새 했어. ("It got urgent at the last second, so I pulled an all-nighter."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.ko: 발등에 불 떨어지고 나서야 부랴부랴 짐을 쌌어요.

examples.en: Everyone ran to the meeting room like it was an emergency.

entries.nuance: Literally 'fire falls on the top of your foot' — when fire lands on your foot you jump instantly, so it means something has suddenly become urgent and you have to deal with it right now. It often carries a self-aware, procrastinator's tone ('I only act once it's an emergency'). Casual-to-polite, extremely common at work and around deadlines.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't read it literally as a burn injury — it's about sudden urgency, not pain.
It's 발등 (top of the foot), not 발 — and 떨어지다 means 'falls,' so keep the whole phrase intact.

entries.english: to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')
entries.shortExplanation: 코앞이다 is a practical expression meaning "to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')".
entries.explanation: "to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')" — that is 코앞이다 (koapida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 시험이 코앞이야, 큰일 났어. ("The exam is right around the corner — I'm in trouble."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 코앞이다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: The exam is right around the corner — I'm in trouble.
The deadline's right on top of us, so it's hectic.
The convenience store is right there but I'm too lazy to go.
It was right under my nose and I still couldn't find it.
usagePhrases.note: 코앞에 두다 = to have right in front of you

examples.ko: 이사 날짜가 코앞이라 짐 싸느라 바빠요.
examples.romanization: isa naljjaga koapira jim ssaneura bappayo.
examples.en: Moving day is almost here, so I'm busy packing.

examples.ko: 설날이 코앞인데 기차표를 아직 못 구했어.
examples.romanization: seolnari koapinde gichapyoreul ajing mot guhaesseo.
examples.en: Lunar New Year is around the corner and I still can't get a train ticket.
The office is right by my place — five minutes on foot.

entries.nuance: Literally 'right in front of the nose,' 코앞 means something is extremely near — either in time (a deadline/event almost here) or in distance (a place very close by). Casual-to-polite and used constantly in daily life. With time it adds a sense of pressure ('no time left'); with distance it stresses how close and convenient something is.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Write 코앞 as one word, not 코 앞.
Context decides whether it means 'soon' (time) or 'nearby' (distance) — don't assume only one.

entries.english: to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')
entries.shortExplanation: 등골이 오싹하다 is a practical expression meaning "to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')".
entries.explanation: 등골이 오싹하다 (deunggori ossakada) = "to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그 얘기 듣고 등골이 오싹했어. ("I got chills down my spine hearing that."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 등골이 오싹하다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.romanization: bame honja geu gil georeunikka deunggori ossakadeoragoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Walking that road alone at night gave me the shivers.

usagePhrases.ko: 사고 영상 보니까 등골이 다 오싹해.
usagePhrases.romanization: sago yeongsang bonikka deunggori da ossakae.
usagePhrases.en: Watching the accident footage sent a total chill down my spine.
Just thinking about it sends a chill down my back.

examples.romanization: gongpo yeonghwaeseo gapjagi soriga naseo deunggori ossakaesseoyo.
examples.en: A sudden sound in the horror movie sent chills down my spine.

examples.ko: 하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했다고 생각하니 등골이 오싹해.
examples.romanization: hamateomyeon keunil nal ppeonhaetdago saenggakani deunggori ossakae.
examples.en: Thinking I almost got into real trouble gives me the chills.

examples.ko: 그 사람 눈빛이 너무 차가워서 등골이 오싹했어요.
examples.romanization: geu saram nunbichi neomu chagawoseo deunggori ossakaesseoyo.
examples.en: His gaze was so cold it sent a shiver down my spine.

entries.nuance: 등골 is the line of your spine, and 오싹하다 is that sudden cold-shiver feeling, so together they describe chills running down your back from fear, dread, or creepiness. Use it for horror, scary stories, or the jolt of realizing you narrowly avoided disaster. Casual-to-polite. The near-synonym 등골이 서늘하다 ('spine goes cool') has the same chilling feel.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's about fear/dread chills, not feeling physically cold from weather.
Pair 등골 with 오싹하다 or 서늘하다 — don't swap in unrelated 춥다 ('cold').

entries.english: to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)
entries.shortExplanation: 입에 침이 마르다 is a practical expression meaning "to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)".
entries.explanation: 입에 침이 마르다 (ibe chimi mareuda) means "to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 엄마가 너 칭찬을 입에 침이 마르게 하더라. ("Mom couldn't stop singing your praises."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 입에 침이 마르다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Mom couldn't stop singing your praises.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; usually 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하다

usagePhrases.ko: 사장님이 그 직원을 입에 침이 마르도록 칭찬하셨어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: sajangnimi geu jigwoneul ibe chimi mareudorok chingchanhasyeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: The boss praised that employee to no end.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; 마르도록 is the common form

usagePhrases.ko: 다들 그 식당을 입에 침이 마르게 추천해.
usagePhrases.romanization: dadeul geu sikdangeul ibe chimi mareuge chucheonhae.

usagePhrases.ko: 입에 침이 마르게 자랑하던데 진짜 좋은가 봐.
usagePhrases.romanization: ibe chimi mareuge jaranghadeonde jinjja joeunga bwa.
usagePhrases.en: They bragged about it endlessly, so it must be really good.

examples.ko: 선생님이 네 그림을 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하셨어.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimi ne geurimeul ibe chimi mareuge chingchanhasyeosseo.
examples.en: The teacher praised your drawing to the skies.

examples.ko: 친구가 그 카페를 입에 침이 마르도록 얘기해서 가 봤어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga geu kapereul ibe chimi mareudorok yaegihaeseo ga bwasseoyo.
examples.en: My friend raved about that cafe so much that I went.

examples.ko: 할머니는 손주 얘기만 나오면 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하세요.
examples.romanization: halmeonineun sonju yaegiman naomyeon ibe chimi mareuge chingchanhaseyo.
examples.en: Grandma gushes nonstop whenever her grandkids come up.

entries.nuance: Literally 'the saliva in the mouth dries up' — if you talk about how great something is long enough, your mouth runs dry, so it means to praise lavishly and tirelessly. Almost always used with 칭찬하다 ('praise'), 자랑하다 ('brag'), or 추천하다 ('recommend') in the form 입에 침이 마르게/마르도록. Casual-to-polite, warm tone.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It means praising endlessly, not literally being thirsty or having a dry mouth.
Don't drop the verb — it's used as 입에 침이 마르게 + (칭찬하다/자랑하다), not on its own.

entries.english: to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')
entries.shortExplanation: 손발이 맞다 is a practical expression meaning "to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')".
entries.explanation: "to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')" — that is 손발이 맞다 (sonbari matda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 우리 둘은 손발이 잘 맞아. ("The two of us work together really well."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: The two of us work together really well.

usagePhrases.en: I'm in sync with the new team, so work goes smoothly.

usagePhrases.ko: 손발이 안 맞아서 자꾸 실수가 나.
usagePhrases.romanization: sonbari an majaseo jakku silsuga na.
usagePhrases.en: We're out of sync, so mistakes keep happening.

usagePhrases.ko: 오래 같이 일하니까 손발이 척척 맞네.
usagePhrases.romanization: orae gachi ilhanikka sonbari cheokcheong manne.
usagePhrases.en: We've worked together so long we're perfectly in sync.

examples.ko: 주방이랑 홀이 손발이 맞아야 장사가 잘돼요.
examples.romanization: jubangirang hori sonbari majaya jangsaga jaldwaeyo.
examples.en: The kitchen and the floor have to be in sync for business to run well.

examples.ko: 둘이 손발이 맞아서 행사를 무사히 끝냈어.
examples.romanization: duri sonbari majaseo haengsareul musahi kkeunnaesseo.
examples.en: The two were in sync and pulled off the event without a hitch.

examples.ko: 처음엔 손발이 안 맞았는데 이제 호흡이 잘 맞아요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumen sonbari an majanneunde ije hoheubi jal majayo.
examples.en: At first we were out of sync, but now we work in great harmony.
examples.note: 호흡이 맞다 is a close synonym

entries.nuance: Literally 'hands and feet match,' it describes two or more people coordinating smoothly — their actions line up like a well-rehearsed team. It's about working rhythm and cooperation, not friendship. Casual-to-polite, very common at work and on any team. The opposite 손발이 안 맞다 means people keep getting in each other's way, and 호흡이 맞다 ('breathing matches') is a near-synonym.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Use it for teamwork/coordination, not for romantic compatibility (that's 잘 어울리다 or 궁합이 맞다).
It needs two or more people — you can't be 손발이 맞다 by yourself.

entries.english: to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')
entries.shortExplanation: 발 벗고 나서다 is a practical expression meaning "to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')".
entries.explanation: 발 벗고 나서다 (bal beotgo naseoda) = "to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 네가 발 벗고 나서 줘서 진짜 고마워. ("Thank you for stepping up and really pitching in."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Thank you for stepping up and really pitching in.

usagePhrases.romanization: hoesaga bal beotgo naseoseo munjereul haegyeolhaesseo.
usagePhrases.en: The company actively stepped in and solved the problem.

usagePhrases.en: He's the type to drop everything to help a friend.

examples.ko: 선배가 발 벗고 나서서 취업을 도와줬어요.
examples.romanization: seonbaega bal beotgo naseoseo chwieobeul dowajwosseoyo.
examples.en: A senior went all in to help me find a job.

examples.ko: 다들 발 벗고 나서서 이사를 도와줘서 금방 끝났어.
examples.romanization: dadeul bal beotgo naseoseo isareul dowajwoseo geumbang kkeunnasseo.
examples.en: Everyone pitched in wholeheartedly with the move, so it finished fast.

examples.ko: 그 문제는 아무도 발 벗고 나서지 않아서 오래 방치됐어요.
examples.romanization: geu munjeneun amudo bal beotgo naseoji anaseo orae bangchidwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Nobody stepped up for that issue, so it was left alone for ages.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to take off your shoes and step forward' — back when shoes were precious, taking them off to wade in showed you were ready to get fully involved, so it means to step up and help eagerly, not half-heartedly. It praises someone for taking initiative for others. Casual-to-polite, warm and approving. Spacing: 발 벗고 나서다 (three words).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mind the spacing: 발 벗고 나서다, not 발벗고 나서다.
It implies wholehearted, voluntary effort to help — don't use it for reluctant or forced help.

entries.english: to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')
entries.shortExplanation: 어깨가 무겁다 is a practical expression meaning "to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')".
entries.explanation: 어깨가 무겁다 (eokkaega mugeopda) means "to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 책임이 커서 어깨가 무거워. ("The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 어깨가 무겁다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it.
I've taken on an important task, so I feel the responsibility.
As the breadwinner, I carry a heavy load.

usagePhrases.ko: 기대가 큰 만큼 어깨가 더 무거워.
usagePhrases.romanization: gidaega keun mankeum eokkaega deo mugeowo.
usagePhrases.en: The bigger the expectations, the heavier the burden.

examples.en: Becoming team lead made the responsibility feel heavier.

examples.ko: 다들 나만 믿는다고 하니까 어깨가 무거워.
examples.romanization: dadeul naman minneundago hanikka eokkaega mugeowo.
examples.en: Everyone says they're counting on me, so I feel the weight.

examples.ko: 큰 프로젝트를 혼자 맡아서 어깨가 너무 무거워요.
examples.romanization: keun peurojekteureul honja mataseo eokkaega neomu mugeowoyo.
examples.en: I'm handling a big project alone, so the burden feels heavy.

entries.nuance: Literally 'heavy shoulders,' it expresses the psychological weight of responsibility or expectation pressing down on you. It's a humble, common way to acknowledge that a duty feels serious — you'll hear it in acceptance speeches, new-role announcements, and everyday talk about pressure. Casual-to-polite/formal. The relief version is 어깨가 가벼워지다 ('shoulders get lighter').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's about emotional/responsibility burden, not literal shoulder pain or stiffness (that's 어깨가 결리다/아프다).
Don't confuse with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which means feeling discouraged or dejected.

entries.english: to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')
entries.shortExplanation: 얼굴이 두껍다 is a practical expression meaning "to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')".
entries.explanation: "to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')" — that is 얼굴이 두껍다 (eolguri dukkeopda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 걔 진짜 얼굴 두껍다, 또 부탁하네. ("He's got some nerve — asking for a favor again."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 얼굴이 두껍다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.romanization: gyae jinjja eolgul dukkeopda, tto butakane.
usagePhrases.en: He's got some nerve — asking for a favor again.
Asking for that takes a lot of nerve.

usagePhrases.ko: 나도 좀 얼굴 두꺼워져야 하나 봐.
usagePhrases.romanization: nado jom eolgul dukkeowojyeoya hana bwa.
usagePhrases.en: Maybe I need to grow a thicker skin.
usagePhrases.note: Self-talk — wishing to be less self-conscious

usagePhrases.en: He's so brazen he doesn't even feel sorry.

examples.ko: 얼굴이 두꺼워서 거절을 당해도 또 시도해요.
examples.romanization: eolguri dukkeowoseo geojeoreul danghaedo tto sidohaeyo.
examples.en: He's thick-skinned, so even after a no he tries again.

examples.ko: 그렇게 민폐 끼치고도 태연한 거 보면 얼굴 두껍다.
examples.romanization: geureoke minpye kkichigodo taeyeonhan geo bomyeon eolgul dukkeopda.
examples.en: Causing all that trouble and staying calm — what nerve.

examples.ko: 면접 땐 얼굴이 좀 두꺼워야 떨지 않아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop ttaen eolguri jom dukkeowoya tteolji anayo.
examples.en: For interviews you need a bit of thick skin so you don't get nervous.

entries.nuance: Literally 'thick face,' it means shameless or brazen — someone who isn't embarrassed when they should be. Usually mildly negative or teasing, though it can flip positive to mean 'not easily flustered' (e.g. for interviews or public speaking). Casual-to-polite. Blunter, harsher variants are 낯이 두껍다 and 낯짝이 두껍다, and the noun for the trait is 철면피.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Nothing to do with literal skin thickness on the face — it's about shamelessness.
Tone matters: it can sound insulting, so don't say it bluntly to someone you must stay polite with.

entries.english: to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')
entries.shortExplanation: 눈코 뜰 새 없다 is a practical expression meaning "to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')".
entries.explanation: 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (nunko tteul sae eopda) = "to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 요즘 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠. ("I'm so swamped these days I can't even catch a breath."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 눈코 뜰 새 없다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: I'm so swamped these days I can't even catch a breath.

usagePhrases.romanization: yeonmarira nunko tteul sae eopsi jinaego isseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: It's year-end, so I'm run off my feet.

usagePhrases.romanization: ae dul kiuneura nunko tteul saega eopseo.
usagePhrases.en: Raising two kids leaves me no time to breathe.

usagePhrases.romanization: opeun siganen nunko tteul sae eopsi sonnimi millyeowa.
usagePhrases.en: At opening time customers pour in nonstop.

examples.ko: 이사하고 정리하느라 눈코 뜰 새 없었어요.
examples.romanization: isahago jeongnihaneura nunko tteul sae eopseosseoyo.
examples.en: I was swamped moving and unpacking.

examples.ko: 행사 준비로 일주일 내내 눈코 뜰 새 없이 일했어.
examples.romanization: haengsa junbiro iljuil naenae nunko tteul sae eopsi ilhaesseo.
examples.en: I worked flat out all week preparing for the event.

examples.ko: 식당이 점심엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠서 정신이 하나도 없어요.
examples.romanization: sikdangi jeomsimen nunko tteul sae eopsi bappaseo jeongsini hanado eopseoyo.
examples.en: The restaurant is so slammed at lunch I can't think straight.

entries.nuance: Literally 'no gap to even open your eyes and nose,' it's a vivid way to say you're so busy you can't spare a second — busier than just 바쁘다. It's almost always used adverbially as 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁘다 ('busy without a moment to breathe'). Casual-to-polite, extremely common when describing a hectic stretch at work or home.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Keep the spacing 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (눈코 is one word; 뜰 새 = 'a moment to open').
It's an intensity phrase usually attached to 바쁘다 — don't use it to mean simply 'I have no time' in a neutral way.

entries.english: to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')
entries.shortExplanation: 바가지를 쓰다 is a practical expression meaning "to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')".
entries.explanation: 바가지를 쓰다 (bagajireul sseuda) means "to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 관광지에서 완전 바가지 썼어. ("I got totally ripped off at the tourist spot."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 바가지를 쓰다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: I got totally ripped off at the tourist spot.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; 바가지(를) 쓰다 = the buyer overpays

usagePhrases.ko: 택시 타다가 바가지 쓴 것 같아요.
usagePhrases.romanization: taeksi tadaga bagaji sseun geot gatayo.
usagePhrases.en: I think I got overcharged in the taxi.

usagePhrases.ko: 여기 비싸니까 바가지 쓰지 않게 가격 먼저 물어봐.
usagePhrases.romanization: yeogi bissanikka bagaji sseuji anke gagyeong meonjeo mureobwa.
usagePhrases.en: It's pricey here, so ask the price first to avoid getting fleeced.
The owner ripped the foreigner off.
usagePhrases.note: 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the seller does the overcharging

examples.ko: 축제 음식이 평소의 두 배라 바가지 쓴 기분이었어요.
examples.romanization: chukje eumsigi pyeongsoui du baera bagaji sseun gibunieosseoyo.
examples.en: The festival food was double the usual price — felt like a ripoff.
I bought it without knowing the going rate and got overcharged.

examples.ko: 흥정 안 하면 시장에서 바가지 쓰기 쉬워요.
examples.romanization: heungjeong an hamyeon sijangeseo bagaji sseugi swiwoyo.
examples.en: If you don't haggle you can easily get fleeced at the market.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to wear a gourd dipper,' it means to be charged way more than something is worth — to get ripped off. Very common when talking about tourist traps, taxis, markets, and festivals. Casual-to-polite. Watch the pair: 바가지(를) 쓰다 = you (the buyer) overpay; 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the seller rips someone off. Often shortened to just 바가지.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't reverse the verbs: 쓰다 = you got ripped off; 씌우다 = you (or the seller) ripped someone off.
It refers to being overcharged, not to a bad-quality product (that's just 별로다 / 안 좋다).

entries.english: you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')
entries.shortExplanation: 국물도 없다 is a practical expression meaning "you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')".
entries.explanation: "you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')" — that is 국물도 없다 (gungmuldo eopda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 한 번만 더 늦으면 국물도 없어. ("Be late one more time and you'll get nothing from me."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 국물도 없다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.romanization: han beonman deo neujeumyeon gungmuldo eopseo.
usagePhrases.en: Be late one more time and you'll get nothing from me.

usagePhrases.ko: 약속 안 지키면 국물도 없을 줄 알아.
usagePhrases.romanization: yaksok an jikimyeon gungmuldo eopseul jul ara.
usagePhrases.en: If you break the promise, don't expect anything good.
Even though I helped this time, I got nothing out of it.

usagePhrases.ko: 그렇게 해 봤자 너한테 국물도 없어.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureoke hae bwatja neohante gungmuldo eopseo.
usagePhrases.en: Even if you do that, there's nothing in it for you.

examples.ko: 사장님이 또 실수하면 국물도 없다고 하셨어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi tto silsuhamyeon gungmuldo eopsdago hasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The boss said if it happens again there'll be no mercy.

examples.ko: 내 말 안 들으면 다음부턴 국물도 없을 거야.
examples.romanization: nae mal an deureumyeon daeumbuteon gungmuldo eopseul geoya.
examples.en: If you don't listen to me, next time you'll get nothing.

examples.ko: 밤새 도왔는데 고맙단 말도 없고, 정말 국물도 없네.
examples.romanization: bamsae dowanneunde gomapdan maldo eopsgo, jeongmal gungmuldo eopsne.
examples.en: I helped all night and didn't even get a thanks — nothing to show for it.

entries.nuance: Literally 'not even broth (국물) left,' it means there's nothing to be gained — no benefit, leftover, or mercy. It's most often a half-joking warning or threat ('do that and you'll get nothing from me'), but can also describe an effort that paid off with zero reward. Casual register; the threat usage sounds blunt, so it's for friends, family, or clearly informal settings.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Nothing to do with actual soup — 국물 here means 'leftover benefit/payoff.'
The threatening tone is informal and can sound harsh; don't use it in polite or professional contexts.

entries.english: to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')
entries.shortExplanation: 찬물을 끼얹다 is a practical expression meaning "to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')".
entries.explanation: 찬물을 끼얹다 (chanmureul kkieonda) = "to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 분위기 좋았는데 걔가 찬물을 끼얹었어. ("The mood was great but he threw cold water on it."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 찬물을 끼얹다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: The mood was great but he threw cold water on it.

usagePhrases.ko: 좋은 소식에 찬물을 끼얹고 싶진 않지만요.
usagePhrases.romanization: joeun sosige chanmureul kkieonjgo sipjin anchimanyo.
usagePhrases.en: I don't mean to rain on the good news, but…

usagePhrases.ko: 다들 신났는데 그 말 한마디가 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: dadeul sinnanneunde geu mal hanmadiga chanmureul kkieonjeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Everyone was excited, but that one comment killed it.
usagePhrases.note: A single remark ruining the mood

usagePhrases.ko: 계획에 자꾸 찬물 끼얹지 말고 좀 응원해 줘.
usagePhrases.romanization: gyehoege jakku chanmul kkieonjji malgo jom eungwonhae jwo.
usagePhrases.en: Stop pouring cold water on the plan and cheer me on.
usagePhrases.note: Asking someone to stop being negative

examples.ko: 회의 분위기가 살아나려는데 부장님이 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui bunwigiga saranaryeoneunde bujangnimi chanmureul kkieonjeosseoyo.
examples.en: The meeting was warming up, but the manager threw cold water on it.

examples.ko: 다 같이 여행 가자던 분위기에 한 명이 찬물을 끼얹었어.
examples.romanization: da gachi yeohaeng gajadeon bunwigie han myeongi chanmureul kkieonjeosseo.
examples.en: Someone threw cold water on the whole let's-go-on-a-trip vibe.

examples.ko: 축하 자리에 굳이 찬물을 끼얹는 말을 할 필요는 없잖아.
examples.romanization: chuka jarie guji chanmureul kkieonjneun mareul hal piryoneun eopsjana.
examples.en: There's no need to say something that ruins a celebration.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to pour cold water over (something hot),' it means to suddenly kill an upbeat mood, excitement, or momentum — usually with a negative comment or unwelcome news. Use it for the person or remark that deflates a good vibe. Casual-to-polite. It's close to 김(을) 빼다 / 김새다 ('to deflate excitement'), but 찬물을 끼얹다 stresses an active, deliberate buzzkill.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling: it's 끼얹다 (kki-eon-da), an easy verb to misspell — not 끼언다 or 끼엊다.
It implies actively spoiling a positive mood, so don't use it for just any bad news; there needs to be enthusiasm or momentum to ruin.

entries.english: Please hold (don't hang up), and wait a moment
entries.shortExplanation: 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please hold (don't hang up), and wait a moment".
entries.explanation: "Please hold (don't hang up), and wait a moment" — that is 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 (kkeunchi malgo gidaryeo juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 ("Please don't hang up and hold on"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Please don't hang up and hold on
usagePhrases.note: full polite form, said to a caller

usagePhrases.en: Please stay on the line for a moment

examples.ko: 담당자 확인해 드릴게요. 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요.
examples.romanization: damdangja hwaginhae deurilgeyo. kkeunchi malgo gidaryeo juseyo.
examples.en: I'll check with the person in charge. Please hold.

examples.ko: 끊지 마시고 잠시만 기다려 주세요. 바로 연결해 드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: kkeunchi masigo jamsiman gidaryeo juseyo. baro yeongyeolhae deurigetseumnida.
examples.en: Please hold a moment; I'll connect you right away.
I'll ask Mom. Don't hang up, hold on.

entries.nuance: What an agent or whoever answered says when they need to step away briefly but want you to stay on the line. 끊다 literally means 'to cut/sever,' which is how Korean expresses hanging up. The -지 말고 ('don't ~ and') warns against hanging up while 기다려 주세요 asks you to wait — together it's the standard 'please hold.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 끊다 (hang up) with 끄다 (turn off) — phones get 끊어, devices get 꺼.
Dropping 주세요 and just saying 끊지 말고 기다려 to a customer — sounds like an order.

entries.shortExplanation: 메모 남겨 드릴까요? is a practical expression meaning "Shall I take a message (for them)?".
entries.explanation: 메모 남겨 드릴까요? (memo namgyeo deurilkkayo?) = "Shall I take a message (for them)?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 메모 남겨 드릴까요? ("Would you like me to leave a message?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.ko: 지금 자리에 안 계세요. 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: jigeum jarie an gyeseyo. memo namgyeo deurilkkayo?
examples.en: They're not at their desk right now. Shall I take a message?
They're in a meeting — would you like to leave a message?

examples.ko: 형 지금 없는데, 메모 남겨 줄까?
examples.romanization: hyeong jigeum eopsneunde, memo namgyeo julkka?
examples.en: Bro's not here — want me to pass on a message?

entries.nuance: Said by whoever answers when the person you want is unavailable, offering to write down a message. 드리다 is the humble verb for 'give/do for someone,' so 남겨 드릴까요? politely offers to do the favor of taking a note for the absent party. This is the natural service-register way to handle a missed connection.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 남겨 줄까요? to a customer — 드릴까요? is more appropriately humble.
Writing 남기다 as 남끼다; the verb stem is 남기- (남겨 = 남기 + 어).

entries.english: I'll connect you (transfer your call)
entries.shortExplanation: 연결해 드릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll connect you (transfer your call)".
entries.explanation: 연결해 드릴게요 (yeongyeolhae deurilgeyo) means "I'll connect you (transfer your call)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 연결해 드릴게요 ("I'll put you through"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 연결해 드릴게요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: I'll connect you to the right department

usagePhrases.note: 반말 / passing the phone to someone

examples.en: I'll connect you to tech support. One moment.

examples.ko: 제가 처리할 수 없는 건이라, 담당자에게 연결해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jega cheorihal su eopsneun geonira, damdangjaege yeongyeolhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: This isn't something I can handle, so I'll transfer you to the right person.

examples.ko: 아, 그건 누나가 알아. 연결해 줄게.
examples.romanization: a, geugeon nunaga ara. yeongyeolhae julge.
examples.en: Oh, my sister knows that. I'll put her on.

entries.nuance: The phrase agents use to transfer your call to another line or department. 연결하다 = 'to connect/link'; 해 드릴게요 makes it a humble promise to do it for you. You'll hear 연결해 드리겠습니다 in the most formal call centers, while 연결해 줄게 works casually when you're just handing your phone to someone nearby.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 연결시켜 드릴게요 — the unnecessary causative 시키다 is over-used here; plain 연결해 is cleaner.
Confusing 연결 (connect a call) with 연락 (contact/get in touch) — different actions.

examples.romanization: bujangnim jigeum bujaejungiseyo. memo namgyeo deurilkkayo?
examples.en: The manager is out right now. Shall I take a message?

examples.ko: 부재중 전화가 세 통이나 와 있네.
examples.romanization: bujaejung jeonhwaga se tongina wa inne.
examples.en: Whoa, I've got three missed calls.

examples.ko: 고객님, 담당자가 부재중입니다. 잠시 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: gogaengnim, damdangjaga bujaejungimnida. jamsi hu dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: Sir/Ma'am, the agent is unavailable. We'll contact you again shortly.

entries.nuance: A slightly formal word meaning 'absent / away from one's seat,' used both to explain that someone can't come to the phone and as the label 부재중 전화 for a missed call on your screen. 부재(不在) is Sino-Korean for 'not present,' so it sounds more official than the everyday 없어요. You'll see and hear it constantly in offices and on phones.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Pronouncing it 부제중 — it's 부재중 (재, not 제).
Using it for a friend who just stepped out; 잠깐 나갔어요 is more natural casually.

entries.english: I'll get in touch with you later
entries.shortExplanation: 나중에 연락드릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll get in touch with you later".
entries.explanation: 나중에 연락드릴게요 (najung-e yeollak-deurilgeyo) = "I'll get in touch with you later". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 나중에 연락드릴게요 ("I'll contact you later"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I'll reach out in a bit
I will get back to you

examples.en: I'm a bit busy right now. I'll contact you later.
I'll check and get back to you later.

examples.ko: 나 지금 운전 중이야. 나중에 연락할게.
examples.romanization: na jigeum unjeon jungiya. najunge yeollakalge.
examples.en: I'm driving right now. I'll call you later.

entries.nuance: The polite way to wrap up or postpone contact — you're promising to reach out again. 연락드리다 uses the humble 드리다 ('do for you'), so it raises the listener; with friends it drops to 연락할게. Note it covers both calling and texting, since 연락 means 'contact' in general, not specifically a phone call.

entries.english: The signal is weak / poor reception
entries.shortExplanation: 신호가 약해요 is a practical expression meaning "The signal is weak / poor reception".
entries.explanation: 신호가 약해요 (sinho-ga yakaeyo) means "The signal is weak / poor reception". Say it as one set phrase — for example 신호가 약해요 ("The signal is weak"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.en: Hello? Reception's weak here so I can't hear well.

examples.ko: 지하라서 신호가 약해요. 끊고 다시 걸게요.
examples.romanization: jiharaseo sinhoga yakaeyo. kkeunko dasi geolgeyo.
examples.en: I'm underground so the signal's weak. Let me hang up and call back.

entries.nuance: The natural way to explain why a call sounds bad or keeps dropping — the cellular 신호 ('signal') is 약하다 ('weak'). Koreans also say 신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 ('the signal doesn't get picked up well') for the same idea. Pair it with 잘 안 들려요 to explain that poor reception is why you can't hear.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 사인(sign) for signal — the cell-reception word is 신호.
Saying 신호가 작아요 (small) — strength is 약하다/세다 (weak/strong), not 작다/크다.

entries.english: Can you hear me okay?
entries.shortExplanation: 잘 들리세요? is a practical expression meaning "Can you hear me okay?".
entries.explanation: "Can you hear me okay?" — that is 잘 들리세요? (jal deulliseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잘 들리세요? ("Can you hear me all right?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: The flip side of 잘 안 들려요 — instead of reporting your own trouble, you ask whether the other person can hear you. 들리다 is the intransitive 'to be heard,' and the honorific 들리세요? politely asks about their experience. It's the go-to reception check on calls and video meetings alike.

examples.en: Long time no see. How are you?
Is your family doing well too?
Yes, I am doing well. Thanks.

entries.nuance: 잘 지내요 with a rising tone asks how someone has been living lately, and with a falling tone it answers that you are doing fine.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it with strangers you just met now

lesson.canDo: Use 잘 지내요? naturally in basic everyday communication.
studyFlow: Say 잘 지내요? as one complete chunk.
Read the first example aloud three times. Then hide the English and say the Korean again.
Choose one follow-up sentence from the usage phrases so it becomes a short exchange.
Check whether the expression is safe with strangers, staff, teachers, or only friendly situations.
lesson.teacherNote: Expressions are not built word by word at first. Learn 잘 지내요? as a ready-to-say sentence, then notice the grammar later through related pattern links.
lesson.pronunciationTip: Say it as one smooth phrase: jal jinaeyo. Do not pause between every Korean syllable block.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Know the social situation
beginnerPath.body: Use it in the situation shown in the examples. Korean expressions often depend on who you are talking to, not only on the English translation.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Add one follow-up
beginnerPath.body: A real conversation usually needs one more sentence after 잘 지내요?. Practice the mini dialogue so it does not stay as a single memorized line.

entries.english: Long time no see.
entries.shortExplanation: 오랜만이에요 is a practical expression meaning "Long time no see.".
entries.explanation: "Long time no see." — that is 오랜만이에요 (oraenmanieyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오랜만이에요 ("long time no see"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 오랜만이에요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

examples.en: Oh, long time no see. How have you been?
It has really been a long time.
Long time no see, senior.

entries.nuance: 오랜만이에요 marks that much time has passed since you last met, so you say it as a warm greeting when reuniting with someone.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it for someone you saw yesterday

entries.english: See you again.
entries.shortExplanation: 또 만나요 is a practical expression meaning "See you again.".
entries.explanation: 또 만나요 (tto mannayo) = "See you again.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 또 만나요 ("see you again"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 또 만나요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

examples.en: Today was fun. See you again.
Go safely. See you again.
I will contact you. See you again.

entries.nuance: 또 만나요 means let us meet again, a hopeful goodbye that suggests you want to see the person another time in the future.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it when you will not meet again
